title: Solving the State Equations
intro: The state equation $x' = Ax + Bu$ can be solved exactly. The answer is built from one object, the matrix exponential $e^{At}$: it carries the starting state forward in time, and, folded together with the input, it gives the response to a push. This page derives it, computes it three ways for real examples, and uses it to get the step and impulse responses.

blocks.text: Start with one state

If there is a single state, the equation is $x' = ax + bu$ with numbers $a$ and $b$. With no input, $x' = ax$ has the solution $x(t) = e^{at}x(0)$: the state is multiplied by $e^{at}$, which decays if $a < 0$ and grows if $a > 0$. You can check it by differentiating, since $\frac{d}{dt}e^{at} = a e^{at}$.

With an input there is a neat trick. Multiply the whole equation by $e^{-at}$ and move the $ax$ term to the left: $e^{-at}(x' - ax) = e^{-at}bu$. The left side is exactly the derivative of the product $e^{-at}x$ (product rule: $e^{-at}x' - a e^{-at}x$). So
Integrate from $0$ to $t$, and then multiply by $e^{at}$ to get $x$ alone:

The first term is what the starting state does by itself. The second says: each small push $b\,u(\tau)\,d\tau$ given at time $\tau$ is carried on to time $t$ by the factor $e^{a(t-\tau)}$, and the pushes are added up. It is a convolution of the input with $e^{at}b$, as met on the page Impulse Response and LTI Systems (#/math/convolution/impulse-response). The whole job on this page is to do the same for a state with $n$ numbers.
The matrix exponential

The scalar exponential has the series $e^{at} = 1 + at + \tfrac12 (at)^2 + \tfrac16 (at)^3 + \cdots$. The same series makes sense with a square matrix in place of the number $a$, and that is the definition:

It always converges. Differentiate term by term: the derivative of $A^k t^k/k!$ is $A \cdot A^{k-1}t^{k-1}/(k-1)!$, so $\frac{d}{dt}e^{At} = Ae^{At}$. This is the whole reason it works: $x(t) = e^{At}x(0)$ satisfies $x' = Ax$, and at $t = 0$ the series gives $e^{A \cdot 0} = I$, so $x(0)$ is right. Two more properties follow, and one warning.

items: $e^{A(t+s)} = e^{At}e^{As}$: running for time $t$ then for time $s$ is the same as running for $t + s$. In particular $e^{At}$ is always invertible, with inverse $e^{-At}$.

$e^{A+B} = e^Ae^B$ is true only when $AB = BA$. For matrices that do not commute it is false in general. Example: $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ have $AB \ne BA$, and $e^Ae^B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ but $e^{A+B} = \begin{pmatrix} \cosh 1 & \sinh 1 \\ \sinh 1 & \cosh 1 \end{pmatrix} \approx \begin{pmatrix} 1.543 & 1.175 \\ 1.175 & 1.543 \end{pmatrix}$.

blocks.text: In practice nobody sums the series by hand for a big $t$. We want a closed form, and there are three routes, all shown here for real systems.
Route 1: diagonalise

If $A = PDP^{-1}$ with $D$ diagonal, then $A^k = PD^kP^{-1}$ (the inner $P^{-1}P$ cancel), so the series gives $e^{At} = P\,e^{Dt}P^{-1}$, and $e^{Dt}$ is just the diagonal matrix of $e^{\lambda_i t}$. This is the idea of Diagonalisation and Powers (#/math/eigenvalues/diagonalisation). Take the heavily damped mass, $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -2 & -3 \end{pmatrix}$, whose characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^2 + 3\lambda + 2 = (\lambda + 1)(\lambda + 2)$.

items: Eigenvalue $\lambda = -1$: solve $(A + I)v = 0$, which is $v_2 = -v_1$ from the first row $(1, 1)$. So $v = (1, -1)$.
Eigenvalue $\lambda = -2$: $(A + 2I)v = 0$ has the first row $(2, 1)$, so $v_2 = -2v_1$ and $v = (1, -2)$.

Put the eigenvectors in the columns of $P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$. Its determinant is $-2 + 1 = -1$, so $P^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{-1}\begin{pmatrix} -2 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$.

blocks.text: Now multiply $P\,\mathrm{diag}(e^{-t}, e^{-2t})$ first, which scales the columns of $P$, and then by $P^{-1}$:

blocks.tex: e^{At} = \begin{pmatrix} e^{-t} & e^{-2t} \\ -e^{-t} & -2e^{-2t} \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2e^{-t} - e^{-2t} & e^{-t} - e^{-2t} \\ -2e^{-t} + 2e^{-2t} & -e^{-t} + 2e^{-2t} \end{pmatrix}

blocks.text: Check two things. At $t = 0$ the matrix is $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, as it must be. And its derivative at $t = 0$ should be $A$: the top row gives $(-2 + 2,\ -1 + 2) = (0, 1)$ and the bottom row $(2 - 4,\ 1 - 4) = (-2, -3)$, which is $A$. At $t = 1$ it equals $\begin{pmatrix} 0.600 & 0.233 \\ -0.465 & -0.097 \end{pmatrix}$: the mass released from $(1, 0)$ is, one second later, at $x(1) = (0.600, -0.465)$, the first column.
Route 2: the Laplace transform

Take the Laplace transform of $x' = Ax$ (see Solving Differential Equations (#/math/laplace-transform/differential-equations)): $sX(s) - x(0) = AX(s)$, so $(sI - A)X(s) = x(0)$ and $X(s) = (sI - A)^{-1}x(0)$. Comparing with $x(t) = e^{At}x(0)$ shows that $e^{At}$ and $(sI - A)^{-1}$ are a Laplace pair. For a $2 \times 2$ matrix the inverse is easy: swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, divide by the determinant. For the same heavy mass,

blocks.tex: sI - A = \begin{pmatrix} s & -1 \\ 2 & s + 3 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad (sI - A)^{-1} = \frac{1}{s^2 + 3s + 2}\begin{pmatrix} s + 3 & 1 \\ -2 & s \end{pmatrix}

blocks.text: The determinant is $s(s+3) + 2 = s^2 + 3s + 2 = (s+1)(s+2)$. Take the top right entry, $\frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)} = \frac{1}{s+1} - \frac{1}{s+2}$ (partial fractions: at $s = -1$ the residue is $1/(-1 + 2) = 1$, at $s = -2$ it is $1/(-2+1) = -1$). Its inverse transform is $e^{-t} - e^{-2t}$, which is the top right entry above. The poles of $(sI - A)^{-1}$ are the eigenvalues, so the exponents in $e^{At}$ are always the eigenvalues. This is the same method as Pole Positions and the Time Signal (#/math/laplace-transform/poles-and-time), entry by entry.
Route 3: complex eigenvalues, the RLC circuit

For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$ the eigenvalues are $-1 \pm j$. You could diagonalise with complex numbers, but there is a shortcut. Write $A = -I + N$ with $N = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$. The identity commutes with everything, so $e^{At} = e^{-t}e^{Nt}$. Now square $N$: the entries of $N^2$ are $1 - 2 = -1$ and $2 - 2 = 0$ in the first row, $-1 + 1 = 0$ and $-2 + 1 = -1$ in the second. So $N^2 = -I$, which makes $N$ behave like the imaginary unit. The series for $e^{Nt}$ then splits into the series of cosine and sine:

blocks.tex: e^{Nt} = \cos t\; I + \sin t\; N, \qquad e^{At} = e^{-t}\begin{pmatrix} \cos t + \sin t & 2\sin t \\ -\sin t & \cos t - \sin t \end{pmatrix}

blocks.text: In general a complex pair $\sigma \pm j\omega$ gives terms $e^{\sigma t}\cos\omega t$ and $e^{\sigma t}\sin\omega t$: a rotation, shrinking at rate $\sigma$ (see Complex Eigenvalues and Rotation (#/math/eigenvalues/complex-eigenvalues)). Here $\sigma = -1$ and $\omega = 1$. At $t = 1$ the matrix is $\begin{pmatrix} 0.508 & 0.619 \\ -0.310 & -0.111 \end{pmatrix}$.

The fourth case, a repeated eigenvalue without enough eigenvectors, adds a factor of $t$: $e^{At} = e^{\lambda t}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & t \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ for the block $\begin{pmatrix} \lambda & 1 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{pmatrix}$, so the terms are $te^{\lambda t}$ (see Repeated Eigenvalues and Defective Matrices (#/math/eigenvalues/repeated-eigenvalues)).
The full solution

Now repeat the scalar trick with matrices. Multiply $x' = Ax + Bu$ by $e^{-At}$ on the left. Because $\frac{d}{dt}\left(e^{-At}x\right) = e^{-At}x' - e^{-At}Ax = e^{-At}(x' - Ax)$, the equation becomes $\frac{d}{dt}\left(e^{-At}x\right) = e^{-At}Bu$. Integrate from $0$ to $t$, multiply by $e^{At}$, and use $e^{At}e^{-A\tau} = e^{A(t-\tau)}$:

blocks.tex: x(t) = e^{At}x(0) + \int_0^t e^{A(t-\tau)}B\,u(\tau)\,d\tau, \qquad y(t) = Cx(t) + Du(t)

blocks.text: The first term is the zero-input response (what the starting state does alone). The second is the zero-state response (what the input does from rest). The system is linear, so the two simply add: this is superposition. That is the whole answer to the question 'what does the system do?': every response, in any state-space model, is this formula.
The step response and the resting point

Give the input a constant value $u = 1$ from $t = 0$ (a unit step) and start from rest, $x(0) = 0$. The integral becomes $\int_0^t e^{A(t-\tau)}B\,d\tau = \int_0^t e^{As}B\,ds$. When $A$ is invertible, $\int_0^t e^{As}ds = A^{-1}(e^{At} - I)$, so

If the system is stable, $e^{At} \to 0$ and the state settles at $x_{\mathrm{rest}} = -A^{-1}B$. This is also the point where the velocity is zero: $0 = Ax + B$. The viewer draws it as the red + labelled 'rest'. Three examples.

items: The light mass, $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -4 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, $B = (0, 1)$: $A x + B = 0$ gives $x_2 = 0$ from the first row and $-4x_1 + 1 = 0$ from the second, so $x_{\mathrm{rest}} = (0.25, 0)$ and $y = 0.25$.
The RLC circuit: $0 = 2x_2$ and $0 = -x_1 - 2x_2 + 1$, so $x_{\mathrm{rest}} = (1, 0)$ and $y = 1$. In steady state the current is zero and the capacitor charges to the source voltage.
The two tanks: $0 = -x_1 + 1$ and $0 = x_1 - 0.5x_2$, so $x_1 = 1$ and $x_2 = 2$. Tank 2 settles at level $2$, because its outflow rate $0.5x_2$ must equal the inflow $1$.

blocks.text: The output settles at $y = Cx_{\mathrm{rest}} = -CA^{-1}B$, the steady-state gain (the DC gain). If $A$ is singular the formula fails, and with good reason. The DC motor has $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $0$: there is no resting point for a unit step. The speed $x_2$ settles to $1$ (from $x_2' = -2x_2 + 2$) but the angle $x_1$, whose rate is $x_2$, keeps growing.

blocks.text: The System is the heavily damped mass, Input unit step, $x(0) = (0, 0)$. The red + labelled 'rest' sits at $(0.5, 0)$, which is $-A^{-1}B$. Watch the path: it leaves the origin straight up along the $x_2$ axis (a push gives velocity first), bulges to the right and creeps into the + without any loop. The poles are real, so there is no oscillation, and the dashed eigen-lines for $\lambda = -1$ and $\lambda = -2$ are drawn through the + as well. The readout ends 'At t = 5 s: x = (0.49, 0.01), y = 0.493'. Step 6 of the walk-through (Next step ▶) sets exactly this input and explains the + in words.
The impulse response

Feed in a very short, very hard push $u = \delta(t)$ from rest. The integral in the full solution then picks out the value at $\tau = 0$: $x(t) = e^{At}B$ for $t > 0$, and $y(t) = Ce^{At}B$. The impulse makes the state jump from $0$ to $B$ at once, and then the free motion takes over from there. The output $Ce^{At}B$ is the impulse response of the system, the function whose convolution with any input gives the output (see Impulse Response and LTI Systems (#/math/convolution/impulse-response) and Convolution (#/math/convolution)).

For the heavy mass, $B = (0, 1)$ picks the second column of $e^{At}$, so $e^{At}B = (e^{-t} - e^{-2t},\ -e^{-t} + 2e^{-2t})$, and $C$ picks the first entry: $y(t) = e^{-t} - e^{-2t}$. For the RLC circuit, $e^{At}B$ is the second column, $e^{-t}(2\sin t,\ \cos t - \sin t)$, so $y(t) = 2e^{-t}\sin t$. The step response is the integral of the impulse response, which gives a check on the heavy mass: $\int_0^t (e^{-s} - e^{-2s})ds = \tfrac12 - e^{-t} + \tfrac12 e^{-2t}$, which tends to $0.5$, the steady-state gain above.

blocks.text: The System is the RLC circuit, Input unit impulse, $x(0) = (0, 0)$. A dashed red line from the origin, labelled 'impulse: x jumps by B', goes to $(0, 1)$ (the inductor current jumps, because the voltage across an inductor is allowed to be huge for an instant). The path then spirals back to the origin, because the poles $-1 \pm j$ are a decaying oscillation. In the time plot the thick red $y$ is the capacitor voltage $2e^{-t}\sin t$: it rises to a peak of about 0.65, crosses zero at $t = \pi \approx 3.14$ s, dips slightly below zero and fades. The readout ends 'At t = 5 s: x = (−0.01, 0.01), y = −0.013'. With Input unit step instead, $y$ ends at 1.005 at $t = 5$ s, the steady-state gain 1 almost reached.

blocks.text: The System is the DC motor, Input unit step, $x(0) = (0, 0)$. There is no red + this time, because $A$ is singular. In the time plot the amber speed $x_2$ rises to 1 and stays; the blue angle $x_1$, with the thick red $y$ drawn under it, climbs along a straight line. The readout says 'Poles 0 and −2: on the edge' and ends 'At t = 8 s: x = (7.50, 1.00), y = 7.500'. The state plane is zoomed out to hold the whole path, which runs off to the right and never turns back.
How a computer finds $e^{At}$

Summing the series directly is a poor method when $\|At\|$ is large: the terms grow huge before they shrink, and the rounding errors swamp the answer. The standard remedy, scaling and squaring, uses $e^{A} = \left(e^{A/2^k}\right)^{2^k}$: divide $A$ by a power of two until it is small, sum the series (or a close rational approximation) for the small matrix, then square the result $k$ times. Moler and Van Loan's paper, listed below, surveys these and other methods and explains why diagonalising is dangerous when the eigenvectors are nearly parallel. In Python, scipy.linalg.expm does exactly this.
Practice

blocks.title: The tanks' matrix exponential
blocks.text: Find $e^{At}$ for the two tanks, $A = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 1 & -0.5 \end{pmatrix}$, by diagonalising, and find the free state at $t = 2$ from $x(0) = (1, 0)$.
solution: The eigenvalues are the diagonal entries of the triangular matrix, $-1$ and $-0.5$. For $\lambda = -1$: $(A + I)v = 0$ has rows $(0, 0)$ and $(1, 0.5)$, so $v_1 = -0.5v_2$ and $v = (1, -2)$ (check: $1 + 0.5(-2) = 0$). For $\lambda = -0.5$: $(A + 0.5I)v = 0$ has the first row $(-0.5, 0)$, so $v_1 = 0$ and $v = (0, 1)$.

$P\,\mathrm{diag}(e^{-t}, e^{-0.5t}) = \begin{pmatrix} e^{-t} & 0 \\ -2e^{-t} & e^{-0.5t} \end{pmatrix}$. Times $P^{-1}$: the top row is $(e^{-t},\ 0)$ and the bottom row is $(-2e^{-t} + 2e^{-0.5t},\ e^{-0.5t})$. So $e^{At} = \begin{pmatrix} e^{-t} & 0 \\ 2\left(e^{-0.5t} - e^{-t}\right) & e^{-0.5t} \end{pmatrix}$. At $t = 0$ it is $I$ and the slope of the bottom left entry is $2(-0.5 + 1) = 1$, the entry of $A$: correct.
At $t = 2$ the first column is $(e^{-2},\ 2(e^{-1} - e^{-2})) = (0.1353,\ 2(0.3679 - 0.1353)) = (0.1353, 0.4651)$. Tank 1 has drained to $13.5\%$ and tank 2 has gained $0.465$ of the water from it.

blocks.title: Step response by the formula
blocks.text: For the two tanks with a unit step input and $x(0) = 0$, write $y(t)$ (the level of tank 2) and check the value at $t = 10$ against the viewer's 1.973.
solution: The step input $u = 1$ enters as $B = (1, 0)$. The zero-state response is $x(t) = x_{\mathrm{rest}} - e^{At}x_{\mathrm{rest}}$ with $x_{\mathrm{rest}} = (1, 2)$ (from the three worked resting points above).

Using $e^{At}$ from the previous problem, $e^{At}(1, 2)^{\top}$ has the second entry $2(e^{-0.5t} - e^{-t})\cdot 1 + e^{-0.5t}\cdot 2 = 4e^{-0.5t} - 2e^{-t}$. So $y(t) = x_2(t) = 2 - 4e^{-0.5t} + 2e^{-t}$.

blocks.title: The motor's speed and angle
blocks.text: For the DC motor with a unit step and $x(0) = 0$, solve the two equations directly and check the readout 'x = (7.50, 1.00)' at $t = 8$ s.
solution: The speed equation stands alone: $x_2' = -2x_2 + 2$. With $x_2(0) = 0$ this is a first-order system with rest value $1$ and time constant $0.5$, so $x_2(t) = 1 - e^{-2t}$.
The angle rate is $x_1' = x_2 = 1 - e^{-2t}$. Integrate from $0$: $x_1(t) = t - \tfrac12(1 - e^{-2t})$.
At $t = 8$: $e^{-16} \approx 10^{-7}$, so $x_2 = 1.00$ and $x_1 = 8 - 0.5 = 7.50$. The angle grows like $t - \tfrac12$: a ramp, with no resting point.

blocks.title: Impulse response of the RLC circuit
blocks.text: Find the time at which $y(t) = 2e^{-t}\sin t$ first crosses zero, and its first maximum.
solution: $y = 0$ when $\sin t = 0$, that is $t = \pi \approx 3.14$ s. The first crossing is at $t = \pi$, since $y > 0$ for $0 < t < \pi$.
blocks.answer: Zero at $t = \pi \approx 3.14$ s; maximum $0.645$ at $t = \pi/4 \approx 0.785$ s.

blocks.text: Sources and further reading

items: Katsuhiko Ogata, Modern Control Engineering, 5th edition (Prentice Hall, 2010). Chapter 9 solves the state equation and defines the state-transition matrix.
Chi-Tsong Chen, Linear System Theory and Design, 4th edition (Oxford University Press, 2013). Chapter 4 covers state-space solutions.
Cleve Moler and Charles Van Loan, 'Nineteen dubious ways to compute the exponential of a matrix, twenty-five years later', SIAM Review 45 (2003) 3–49.

Karl Johan Åström and Richard M. Murray, Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers, 2nd edition (Princeton University Press, 2021). Its chapter on linear systems covers the matrix exponential and the solution of the state equations.
